newsitem.title: HONG KONG: HK women queue up for $1,000 Last Empress makeover.
newsitem.headline: HK women queue up for $1,000 Last Empress makeover.

text.p: A young woman slowly turns into China's "Last Empress" -- an exotic beauty with a hint of danger -- under the hands of a makeup artist and hair-designer. It takes an hour, costs US$1,000 and Hong Kong women can't wait.
The extravagant, lurid makeover is in huge demand for partygoers celebrating Hong Kong's July 1 return to China, focus of almost non-stop festivity in this wealthy territory.
Think... vivid scarlet cosmetics, pink and blue-black hair studded with jewel-like flowers, vermilion silk brocade dress slashed to the thigh -- a vision of Hollywood meets the Mystic East.
Add touches of Forbidden City-plus-30s Shanghai decadence, and you have a party outfit that will makes eyes pop.
"It's a dream, just for an evening of a lifetime," says Australia's internationally-known hair-stylist Kim Robinson, who created the look with Hong Kong Chinese makeup artist Alice So.

Robinson, who plans to introduce the world to an everyday "Asian international beauty concept", says: "I have 30 clients waiting for the Empress style and my other stylists are also besieged by interested women."
A ruthless leader in Beijing's fortress palaces, the 19th century Empress Dowager Tzu-hsi (styled in present-day Mandarin as Zi-Ci) is an odd glamour role-model.

She ruled China a century ago in the twilight of the Qing Dynasty, a corrupt, cruel and inefficient administration whose weakness allowed foreign powers, such as Britain in Hong Kong, to nibble away at the fringes of its empire.
The empress, also known as "The Old Buddha", was one of two extraordinary women at the centre of power in the 19th century.

Overseeing the ramshackle Celestial Empire of the world's largest nation, Zi-Ci became one of the most powerful women in Chinese history, while in London Queen Victoria ruled over the now-vanished British Empire, a quarter of the globe.
Both women were dumpy, plain and hard-headed in an era of almost total male political power.

"No, there are no plans to create a Queen Victoria look -- there simply is not the demand," says Robinson, as he and associate So create "The Last Empress looking towards 2001" style on Janet Ma, a 25-year-old Hong Kong super-model.
Janet, a tall, willowy Chinese, arrived in t-shirt, jeans and trainers and within an hour was transformed into a strangely alluring creature guaranteed to halt any party in its tracks.

Robinson says Hong Kong's rich, pampered and beautiful women, the mahjong-playing "tai-tais", are spending fortunes to look like no other women in the world for handover festivities, billed as Asia's "party of the century."
Money buys splendour, as everything else in Hong Kong, one of the richest and most acquisitive societies on earth where wealth is displayed ostentatiously.

Women flock to Hong Kong's exclusive Orient Salon run by Robinson, a West Australian farm boy who joined a Perth hairdressing salon as a teenage odd-job employee and became one of the world's leading hair designers.
He also flies round the world to clients.
Robinson specialises in recreation of Asian beauty, making Oriental women look "international."

Niggling footnote: Historians generally regard Zi-Ci as a monster who specialised in having her enemies thrown down wells. She wasn't even Chinese, being a scion of the alien Manchu dynasty (1644-1911) that subjugated China.
She was probably a supreme party-pooper -- but this is showbusiness, and Hong Kong 1997.
